note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A change to the cutting sequence on a large job must reach six welders on two shifts. Which is the best way to pass it on?
options: Brief both shifts and put the change in writing in the job file
Tell the day shift and ask them to pass it on to the night shift
Send one text message to the night shift leader only
Wait for the weekly meeting and mention it then

questions.stem: Why is it better to ask a welder 'Tell me how you will set up this joint' than 'Do you understand?'
options: It sounds more formal, so the welder takes it more seriously
It shows what the welder really understood, not just a yes
It saves time, because the welder does not need to answer
It means the instruction never needs to be written down

questions.stem: Kemar is leading a team of four to make a set of steel stair stringers. What should he do first when he briefs the team?
options: Hand out the tools and let each person pick a task
Start work himself, so that the others can copy him
Give every detail at once and then leave them to it
Explain the aim of the job and each person's part in it

questions.stem: A new trainee in your team does not yet know the shop's trade terms. What is the best way to instruct her?
options: Speak faster so that she keeps up with the rest of the team
Use plain words, show each step, and check she can do it
Give her the written procedure and leave her to read it
Ask another trainee to explain it to her later in the day

questions.stem: You are giving a 10-minute toolbox talk on grinding disc safety. Which approach works best?
options: Read the maker's whole leaflet aloud, word for word
Cover every safety topic in the shop, so nothing is missed
Keep to one topic, show a real disc, and ask questions
Hold it at the end of the day, after the work is done

questions.stem: Why should a work meeting end with a list of actions, each with a name and a date?
options: So the minutes are longer and look more complete
So the supervisor does not need to give any more orders
So everyone knows who will do what, and by when
So nobody needs to ask questions at the next meeting

questions.stem: In a site meeting, the client and the foreman talk over each other and the point is lost. You are chairing the meeting. What should you do?
options: Let them argue it out, then close the meeting early
Agree with the client, because the client is paying
Drop the topic and move on to the next item
Ask each to speak in turn, then sum up both views

questions.stem: A welder says the new electrodes 'are not running right'. Which question will get you the most useful facts?
options: 'Are you sure you set the machine up properly?'
'Why did you not tell me about this yesterday?'
'What exactly happens when you strike the arc?'
'Do you want me to order a different type?'

questions.stem: Before a lift, you must confirm that the sling is rated for the load. Which question is best?
options: 'How do you feel about this lift today?'
'Is the sling's safe working load more than the load?'
'What do you think about slings in general?'
'Can you tell me about your past lifting jobs?'

questions.stem: Apart from an emergency stop, which anyone may give, why should only one named person give signals to a crane operator during a lift in a noisy yard?
options: So the others can take a break while the lift is done
So the signaller can also hook and unhook the load
So the operator never gets two signals that disagree
So the operator does not need to watch the load

questions.stem: While you explain a weld repair, a welder keeps looking at his phone and nodding without speaking. What is the best response?
options: Carry on, because the nodding shows that he agrees
Pause, and ask him to explain the repair back to you
Tell him off in front of the team for not listening
Give the job to another welder and say nothing

questions.stem: You need to brief two fitters while grinders are running nearby. What is the best way to overcome the noise?
options: Shout the instructions over the sound of the grinders
Use more trade terms, so that the message is shorter
Move to a quiet spot, or pause the noisy work
Text them the brief while they carry on working

questions.stem: Why must a welder read the welding procedure specification (WPS) before starting a job?
options: It lists the prices of all the materials for the job
It records the welder's hours for the payroll clerk
It sets the approved process, filler and settings
It gives the client's address and the delivery dates

questions.stem: Before using a new pickling paste on stainless steel, which part of its safety data sheet (SDS) tells you which gloves and eye protection to wear?
options: The transport and shipping information part
The exposure controls and personal protection part
The ecological and environmental effects part
The disposal and waste considerations part

questions.stem: Which line is best in a handover note to the next shift?
options: 'Gate 2: hinges tacked only. Weld out and grind today.'
'Job is nearly done, with just a few small bits left on it.'
'Somebody needs to look at the gate thing later on.'
'Gate work went OK today, no big problems at all.'

questions.stem: You must write a short report to the manager about a late delivery of steel plate. What should come first?
options: A full story of every phone call you made to the supplier
Your own opinion of the supplier's delivery driver
A list of the other jobs the shop has this month
What is late, how it affects the job, and what you need

questions.stem: You must email a client to say that her railing will be two days late. Which email is best?
options: None at all, because she may not notice the delay
One that blames the supplier in strong words, so she is not angry with you
One that says sorry, gives the reason and the new date
Just 'Railing late. Sorry.' with no new date given

questions.stem: Why should an incident report be written as soon as possible after the event?
options: Details are still fresh, so the facts are more accurate
It means that no investigation is needed afterwards
The report can then be kept from the rest of the staff
It stops the injured person from making a claim

questions.stem: Which line in an incident report states a fact, not an opinion?
options: 'Dwayne was careless and rushing, as usual.'
'The grinder guard was found off, on the bench.'
'The accident was probably the new man's fault.'
'I think this shop is always far too crowded.'

questions.stem: Two welders in your team argue over who should use the only TIG set. As team leader, what should you do first?
options: Give the set to the older welder to keep the peace
Tell them both to sort it out between themselves
Report them both to the manager straight away
Hear each one out and find what each really needs

questions.stem: When you raise poor work with a welder, why is it better to say 'The weld failed the check' than 'You did a bad job'?
options: It is a softer way to hide the fault from the manager
It means that nobody needs to repair the weld
It deals with the problem, not the person
It shows the welder clearly who is in charge

questions.stem: What is the best way to give feedback to a trainee whose fillet welds are uneven?
options: Say nothing, and redo the welds yourself after hours
Tell the class that the trainee's welds are the worst
Say what is good, show what to change, agree a retry
Give a general comment such as 'Try harder next time'

questions.stem: The quality inspector rejects one of your welds and explains why. What is the most professional response?
options: Argue until the inspector agrees to pass the weld
Listen, ask which standard applies, and agree the repair
Accept it, but tell your team that the inspector is wrong
Grind the weld out without asking what was wrong

questions.stem: A customer at the shop counter in May Pen asks a technical question you cannot answer. What should you do?
options: Say you will find out, take a number, and call back
Give your best guess so that you look knowledgeable
Tell the customer to search the internet for it
Send the customer to another shop down the road

questions.stem: A client asks for a change to a gate design after work has started. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Agree on the spot and start the change at once
Note it, price it, and confirm it in writing first
Refuse, because no change is allowed once work starts
Make the change, but say nothing about the extra cost

questions.stem: On a large site, which is good practice when using a two-way radio?
options: Hold the button down so that nobody else can cut in
Think first, speak clearly, then wait for a reply
Give long messages with full details of the job
Talk while others are talking, to save time

questions.stem: A supplier phones to say the steel will arrive at 7:30 tomorrow, not 10:00. Why should you read the time back and then send a short text to confirm it?
options: So that the call lasts longer and the supplier pays
Because a phone call can never be an agreement
So that the supplier knows you do not trust them
To avoid a mix-up, and to keep a record of it

questions.stem: Your team includes workers of different ages, faiths and backgrounds. Which is good practice when you communicate?
options: Use nicknames based on where each person comes from
Speak mainly to the workers who are most like you
Treat everyone with respect, and avoid hurtful jokes
Let the oldest workers decide who is told things first

questions.stem: Why should a supervisor ask the welders for their views before changing the shop's work routine?
options: So that the supervisor does not have to decide
They do the work and may spot problems in the plan
So that the change can be blamed on them later
So that the welders can vote to keep the old routine

questions.stem: You find a mistake in the cut list that the drafter gave you. Which is the best way to raise it?
options: Correct it yourself on the sheet and say nothing
Wait and see if anyone else notices it first
Tell the rest of the team the drafter is careless
Show the drafter politely before any cutting

questions.stem: A written work instruction can be read in two different ways. What should you do?
options: Ask the writer what was meant, and note the answer
Choose the quicker meaning and start work on it
Do half of the job one way and the other half the other way
Wait until someone else starts, and copy them

questions.stem: You need to warn others that a newly welded handrail is still hot. Which is the best way?
options: Mark it HOT and tell the people nearby
Trust that people will see that the metal is glowing
Throw water on it so that no warning is needed
Stand next to it for a minute, then walk away

questions.stem: At the start of a shift, why should the team leader confirm each person's task aloud with the whole group?
options: It gives the leader a chance to go over old complaints
It only matters on days when the manager is watching
It shows the team that the leader knows more than them
So no task is missed or done twice

questions.stem: A chart on the shop wall shows the weld reject rate falling from 12% to 4% over a month. What does this tell the team?
options: The team is welding fewer joints each week
The inspector has stopped checking the welds
Nothing, because charts cannot show quality
The quality of the welding has improved

questions.stem: Which is the clearest written instruction for a trainee?
options: 'Prepare the edge in the usual manner as required.'
'Do the bevel like we did that other time, roughly.'
'Edge preparation is to be undertaken where needed.'
'Grind a 30° bevel, leaving a 2 mm root face.'

questions.stem: Where is the best place to find the right current range for a new type of electrode?
options: On the price label stuck on the box
In the maker's data on the packet or data sheet
From a friend who used another type last year
By guessing from the colour of the flux coating

questions.stem: A caller says he is from another company and asks what price you quoted a client. What should you do?
options: Give him the price, as it is only a number
Give a rough figure, so you do not seem rude
Ask him to email so you can send the quote
Politely refuse, and tell your supervisor

questions.stem: You must show three new trainees how to set up an oxy-acetylene cutting torch. Which order is best?
options: Let them try first, then explain what they did wrong
Show them once quickly, then leave them to practise
Give them the manual and test them the next day
Explain, show, let each try while you watch, then check

questions.stem: Why do most workplaces set out who reports to whom (the chain of command)?
options: So problems reach the person who can act on them
So workers never need to speak to the manager
So only the supervisor needs to know the plan
So that blame always falls on the most junior worker

questions.stem: You are sending photos of a weld defect to the engineer by phone. What is best practice?
options: Add a note giving the job, the joint and what the photo shows
Send them with no message, as pictures speak for themselves
Post them in the staff social media group so that all can see
Send twenty blurred photos so that at least one is clear

questions.stem: A visiting engineer uses words you do not understand during a site walk. What should you do?
options: Ask him to explain them, and note them down
Nod along so that you do not look uninformed
Pretend to take a phone call and walk away
Ask a co-worker afterwards to guess what he meant

questions.stem: When you brief your team, which body language helps most?
options: Looking at your notes and speaking quickly
Keeping your hands in your pockets and looking down
Facing the group, with eye contact and a steady pace
Standing with your back to them, pointing at the job

questions.stem: A welder tells you the fume extractor in his bay is not working. What should you do?
options: Thank him, stop welding there if needed, and report it
Tell him to open the door and carry on welding
Say it is not your job and send him to the manager
Promise to look at it next month when the shop is quiet

questions.stem: Why are safe work procedures often written as a numbered list of steps?
options: Numbered lists use more paper, so they look important
Numbers make the steps harder for anyone to change
The order is clear and a worker can find their place
It is the only form a manager is allowed to sign

questions.stem: After a job, how can a team leader best find out whether the team's communication worked?
options: Hold a short review: what went well, what to change
Assume it worked if nobody made a complaint
Count how many emails and texts were sent during the job
Ask only the client what they thought of it

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What one word names the reply or reaction that shows the sender whether a message was understood?
What do the letters SDS stand for, on the sheet that comes with a chemical such as a pickling paste?
On a welding job, what do the letters WPS stand for?
Which crane hand signal must the operator always obey, whoever gives it?
What do we call a short written note left for the next shift about the state of the work?
In an email, what do the letters BCC stand for?
What do we call the line of reporting at work, from worker to supervisor to manager?
What word describes communication by body language, facial expression and gestures, without words?
A drawing is marked 'Rev C'. What word does 'Rev' stand for?
What one word names anything that stops a message being received clearly, such as noise or unclear words?
What do we call a question that can be answered with only 'yes' or 'no'?
When a contractor asks the engineer in writing to make a drawing clear, what do the letters RFI stand for?
On a quality form that records work which does not meet the specification, what do the letters NCR stand for?
What word is said at the end of a two-way radio message to show you have finished and are waiting for a reply?
In a written report, what is the name of the short part at the start that gives the main points in a few lines?

essays.stem: Explain how you would give clear instructions to a team of four for a fabrication job, and how you would check that each person has understood.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would read the job card and drawing myself, so that I know the aim, the steps, the hazards and the quality needed. I would gather the team in a quiet place, away from grinding noise, with the drawing in front of us. I would explain the aim of the job, then the steps in order, then each person's task, using plain words and showing the real part or a sketch. I would point out the hazards and their controls, and the checks that will be made. To check understanding I would not just ask 'Do you understand?'. I would ask each person to tell me in their own words what they will do first and which size or check matters most. I would answer questions, write the key points on the job card or a whiteboard, and check the first piece of work early, so that mistakes are caught before they spread.
markingPoints: Prepares first: reads the job card and drawing, and knows the aim, steps, hazards and quality
Briefs in a quiet place, in plain words, using the drawing or a real part
Gives each person a clear task in a sensible order, with the hazards and checks
Checks understanding with open questions, or by asking each person to explain back
Writes the key points down and checks the first work early

essays.stem: Describe how to plan and lead a 10-minute toolbox talk on a safety topic, such as safe use of an angle grinder.
essays.modelAnswer: I would choose one topic linked to the work the team is doing that day, such as angle grinders. I would plan three or four key points, for example: check that the disc is the right type and speed rating for the grinder and is not damaged; keep the guard on; wear a face shield, safety glasses and ear protection; and unplug the grinder before changing a disc. I would bring a real grinder, unplugged, and a damaged disc to show. I would hold the talk at the start of the shift, in a quiet place, standing where everyone can see and hear me. I would speak in plain words, keep it short and ask questions such as 'What would you check before fitting a disc?'. I would let the team share their own near misses. At the end I would sum up the key points, have everyone sign the attendance sheet, and note any problems raised so that they are fixed.
markingPoints: Chooses one topic that fits the work being done
Plans a few clear key points and brings a real item to show
Holds it at the start of the shift where everyone can see and hear
Involves the team with questions and their own experience
Sums up, records attendance and follows up the issues raised

essays.stem: Explain the main barriers to communication in a welding and fabrication shop, and how a team leader can overcome each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Noise from grinders, hammers and machines makes speech hard to hear. The leader can brief people in a quiet place, pause noisy work for a moment, or use agreed hand signals. PPE such as helmets and ear protection also blocks sound and hides faces, so the leader should get the person's attention first and check they have heard. Trade terms confuse new trainees, so the leader should use plain words and explain each term the first time it is used. Workers may be tired, rushed or worried, so the leader should choose a good time and keep messages short. Some people are shy to say they did not understand, so the leader should ask open questions and make it safe to ask. Messages passed from person to person get changed, so important instructions should be given directly and put in writing. On a large site, distance can be overcome with radios used correctly.
markingPoints: Names noise and PPE as barriers, with fixes such as a quiet place, a pause or hand signals
Names trade terms or language level, with plain words and explanation as the fix
Names personal barriers such as tiredness, stress or shyness, with a fix
Names messages that change when passed on, with direct and written instructions as the fix
Shows that the leader still checks understanding once the barrier is dealt with

essays.stem: Two members of your team are in conflict over sharing equipment, and it is slowing the job down. Describe how you would handle it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would act early, before the conflict grows. First I would make sure the work is safe and stop any shouting on the shop floor. Then I would speak to each person in private and let them explain, listening without taking sides and asking questions to find the real problem, for example that both need the plasma cutter in the morning to meet their own targets. I would then bring them together and keep the talk on the job and the facts, not on personal remarks, and ask them to suggest solutions. We might agree booking times for the machine, change the order of tasks so they do not need it at the same time, or ask the supervisor for a second machine. I would write down what was agreed, tell the rest of the team if it affects them, and check a few days later that it is working. If the conflict continued, I would report it to my supervisor.
markingPoints: Acts early and keeps the work area safe and calm
Listens to each person in private without taking sides
Keeps the discussion on the facts and the job, not on the people
Agrees a practical solution with both, such as booking times or a new order of work
Records the agreement, follows up, and refers to the supervisor if it continues

essays.stem: Describe how to write a short report to the manager about a problem on a job, such as a batch of rejected welds. Say what it should contain and why.
essays.modelAnswer: The report should start with a clear title, the date, the job number, and who it is to and from. The first lines should give the main point, for example: '8 of the 20 brackets for job 2417 failed visual inspection on 3 November because of porosity.' Then it should give the facts in order: what was found, when, by whom and how it was checked, keeping facts apart from opinions. Next it should give the likely cause, such as damp electrodes or a draught across the bay, and how this was found. Then it should say what has been done and what is proposed, such as repairing the welds, drying the electrodes and screening the bay, with names and dates. It should end with any help or decision needed from the manager. Plain words, short sentences and headings help the manager read it quickly and act on it. Photos or the inspection sheet can be attached as evidence.
markingPoints: Clear heading details: title, date, job number, to and from
The main point first, in a sentence or two
The facts in order, kept apart from opinions
The cause, the actions taken and the actions proposed, with names and dates
Plain words and headings, with evidence such as photos or inspection sheets attached

essays.stem: Explain how to give useful feedback to a trainee about poor work, and how you should receive feedback on your own work.
essays.modelAnswer: Feedback should be given soon after the work, in private, and about the work, not the person. I would start with something the trainee did well, then say exactly what needs to change, for example: 'The fillet legs are uneven: 5 mm on the top plate and 8 mm on the bottom.' I would show the likely cause, such as the electrode angle, and demonstrate the correct way. Then we would agree a next step, such as two more practice runs while I watch, and I would praise the improvement. When I receive feedback, I should listen without arguing or making excuses, ask questions to understand which standard was used and what I should change, and thank the person. I should then act on it and check later that the change has worked. Taking feedback well helps me improve and sets the right example for my team.
markingPoints: Gives feedback soon, in private, about the work and not the person
Starts with a good point, then gives exact facts about what must change
Shows the cause and the correct method, and agrees a next step
Receives feedback by listening, asking questions and not arguing
Acts on the feedback and checks that it has worked

essays.stem: A client phones, upset that her new gate is late. Describe how you would deal with the call and follow it up.
essays.modelAnswer: I would answer politely, give my name and the business name, and let the client explain without interrupting. I would stay calm and show that I understand, for example: 'I am sorry the gate is late. I understand you need it for security.' I would ask questions to get the facts: her name, phone number, the job number and what she was told before. I would read the details back to check them. I would not make promises I cannot keep, and I would not blame other staff. If I cannot answer at once, I would tell her when she will hear from us, for example by 3 p.m. today. After the call I would check the job with the supervisor, then call her back at the time promised with the new date and the reason. I would confirm the new date by text or email, record the complaint and the actions in the job file, and make sure the new date is met.
markingPoints: Answers politely and listens without interrupting, staying calm
Shows understanding and says sorry without blaming others
Gets the key details and reads them back
Gives a realistic time for a reply and does not over-promise
Follows up: checks the job, calls back on time, confirms in writing and records it

essays.stem: Explain how to run a short production meeting so that it is useful, from planning it to following it up.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the meeting I would decide its purpose, who needs to be there and how long it should last, for example 20 minutes. I would send out a short agenda with the topics, such as jobs due this week, material deliveries, and safety and quality issues. At the start I would state the purpose and the finish time. I would take each item in turn, let each person speak, keep people to the point and stop side arguments. One person would take the minutes. For each decision, we would agree who will do it and by when, and the minute-taker would write it in an action list. At the end I would read back the actions to check that everyone agrees. After the meeting the minutes would be sent out or posted within a day. At the next meeting we would start by checking the actions from last time, so that decisions are carried out.
markingPoints: Plans the purpose, the people and the time, and sends an agenda
Starts on time, states the purpose and keeps to the agenda
Gives everyone a chance to speak and keeps the discussion on track
Records decisions as actions with names and dates
Sends the minutes out promptly and checks the actions at the next meeting

essays.stem: Compare spoken, written and visual communication (signs, signals and drawings) on a fabrication job. Say when each is the best choice.
essays.modelAnswer: Spoken communication, face to face, by phone or by radio, is quick and allows questions and instant feedback, so it is best for daily briefings, quick questions and emergencies. Its weakness is that people forget or mishear, and there is no record. Written communication, such as job cards, procedures, reports, emails and handover notes, gives a lasting record that can be checked later. It is best for instructions with sizes and settings, changes to a job, agreements with clients, and reports. Its weakness is that it is slower, and it may be misread if it is not clear. Visual communication, such as safety signs, crane hand signals, drawings and sketches, works where speech fails, for example in a noisy yard or with someone who reads little English. Drawings show shapes and sizes more clearly than words. A good team leader often uses all three together: explains the job aloud, shows the drawing, and puts the key points in writing.
markingPoints: Spoken: quick and allows feedback; best for briefings, questions and emergencies
Written: a lasting record; best for sizes, settings, changes, agreements and reports
Visual: signs, hand signals and drawings work in noise and show shape and size
Gives a weakness of at least two of the types
Explains that the types are often used together

essays.stem: Explain why a team leader should consult the team before changing how work is done, and describe how to do it.
essays.modelAnswer: The people who do the work often know problems that the leader cannot see, such as a machine that is hard to reach or a step that wastes time. Asking them first can make the change safer and better. It also helps the team accept the change, because they feel respected and understand the reasons. Consulting is good safety practice too, because workers must be able to raise hazards. To consult, I would explain the problem and the reason for the change, for example new fume extraction arms that mean moving the welding bays. I would ask for views in a team meeting, and also give people a chance to speak privately or in writing. I would listen, note the ideas and concerns, and answer them honestly. After the decision I would explain what was decided and why, including why some ideas were not used, and review the change after a few weeks.
markingPoints: Workers know the practical problems and can improve the plan
Consulting helps the team accept and follow the change
Explains the reason for the change and asks for views in more than one way
Listens, records the ideas and gives honest answers
Explains the final decision and reviews the change later

practical1.title: Plan and lead a toolbox talk and a job briefing for a fabrication task
practical1.brief: As a group, plan and deliver two short team briefings, as a team leader would on a real job. The assessor gives the group a job card and drawing for a fabrication task (for example, making four steel wall brackets) and a safety topic (for example, angle grinder safety). Part 1, planning (about 1 hour): together, write a one-page job briefing sheet (the aim, the steps in order, who does what, the hazards and controls, and the quality checks) and a short outline for a 10-minute toolbox talk on the safety topic. Part 2, delivery: each member leads one part of the toolbox talk or the job briefing for about 3 minutes while the rest of the group acts as the team. Each speaker must use the drawing or a real item, ask at least two open questions to check understanding, and write the team's questions and the answers on the sheet. Part 3, close-out: the group completes an attendance and sign-off sheet and writes a short review of what went well and what to improve. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the briefing sheet, the talk outline, the sign-off sheet and the review once for the whole group.
materials: Job card and drawing for a fabrication task (from the assessor)
An angle grinder, unplugged, with a good disc and a damaged disc to show
Flip chart or whiteboard and markers
Briefing sheet, talk outline, and attendance and sign-off sheet (blank forms)
photos: The group planning the briefing sheet together
The finished job briefing sheet and toolbox talk outline
Each member leading their part of the briefing (one photo per member)
The drawing or the unplugged grinder being used to make a point
The questions and answers written on the sheet
The signed attendance and sign-off sheet, and the review notes
checklist: Helped to write the briefing sheet, with clear steps, roles, hazards and checks
Led their part in plain words, at a steady pace, facing the group
Used the drawing or a real item to make the point clear
Asked open questions to check understanding, and answered questions correctly
Listened to others without interrupting, and gave useful points in the review
Wrote questions, answers and actions accurately on the sheet
safety: The grinder used to show the points stays unplugged, with its guard fitted
Hold the briefing in the classroom or away from live welding and grinding
Keep walkways and exits clear while the group stands for the talk
Follow the Centre's workshop rules and wear the PPE they require if the briefing is held in the shop

practical2.title: Handle a workplace communication problem: phone call, team meeting and written follow-up
practical2.brief: As a group, deal with a realistic problem from the first phone call to the written follow-up, using role play. The assessor gives a case card: for example, Mrs Campbell of Mandeville phones to complain that her new steel gate rubs on the post and was delivered a week late, and two welders in the team disagree about whose fault it is. Stage 1: one member takes the client's call while another plays the client; the member fills in a phone message and complaint form and reads the details back. Stage 2: the group holds a 15-minute team meeting with a written agenda. One member chairs, one takes the minutes with an action list (names and dates), and the disagreement is dealt with calmly, by the facts. Stage 3: members write (a) a short, polite email or letter to the client with the plan and dates, and (b) a one-page report to the manager with the facts, the likely cause and the actions. Each document is checked by another member before it is final. Stage 4: one member calls the client back (role play) to confirm the plan. Every member takes at least one speaking role and writes or checks at least one document. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and documents to the group's practical.
materials: Case card (from the assessor), with made-up names and details
A computer with a word processor and a practice email account, or lined paper
Pens, and a table and chairs for the meeting
photos: The completed phone message and complaint form
The agenda, and the meeting in progress with the chair and minute-taker
The minutes with the action list
The draft email or letter to the client, with another member's corrections
The final report to the manager
checklist: Spoke politely and clearly, and listened without interrupting
Asked questions to get the facts, and read back the key details
Stayed calm and dealt with the disagreement by the facts, without blame
Took an active part in the meeting; actions were recorded with names and dates
Wrote in plain, correct English, keeping facts apart from opinions
Checked another member's document and suggested useful corrections
Kept the client's details private and filed the documents as told
safety: Hold the role play in the classroom, not on the shop floor
Use only the made-up details on the case card, never real people's personal data
Treat every member with respect during the role play: no personal remarks
Use only the Centre's computers and practice accounts, never personal ones
